long: A crypto wallet does not hold coins. Balances are on-chain state; the wallet stores private keys, or a seed that derives them, and uses them to sign transactions. Whoever can sign controls the funds. So wallet security comes down to two things: guarding the key, and knowing exactly what you sign. Losing the keys means losing access; leaking them means losing the coins. Even with your own keys, one bad signature can empty a wallet. The series covers how wallets work and how people get drained.
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #1: A wallet is a key manager: it stores private keys (or a seed that derives them) and signs transactions. Balances are on-chain state. Whoever can sign controls the funds, so security = guarding the key and what you sign.
simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #1: Your wallet holds no coins. Coins live on the blockchain; your wallet holds the keys that can move them. Lose the keys, lose access. Leak them, lose the coins. Daily: how wallets work and how people get drained.
variant: Crypto #Wallet Security #1: Not your keys, not your coins. But even with your keys, one bad signature can empty a wallet. This series covers what a wallet really does, and every trick used to drain one.

card.title: Your wallet holds keys, not coins
card.sub: Whoever can sign controls the funds. Guard the key and read what you sign.

long: A BIP39 recovery phrase is a random number written as words. The spec allows 128 to 256 bits of entropy (ENT). A checksum of ENT/32 bits, taken from the SHA-256 of the entropy, is appended, and the result is cut into 11-bit chunks, each an index into a 2048-word list. 128 bits gives 12 words with a 4-bit checksum; 256 bits gives 24 words with an 8-bit checksum. Knowing this shows why the words must come from real randomness, not from a person.
tech: Crypto #Wallet Security #2: BIP39: entropy (128 to 256 bits) + a checksum of ENT/32 bits from its SHA-256, cut into 11-bit chunks mapped to a 2048-word list. 128 bits gives 12 words (4-bit checksum); 256 bits gives 24 words (8-bit checksum).
simple: Crypto #Wallet Security #2: A 12-word recovery phrase is just a big random number written in words. Each word comes from a fixed list of 2048 and stores 11 bits. 12 words = 128 bits of randomness plus a small checksum.

card.title: A seed phrase is a random number in words
card.sub: 128 to 256 bits of entropy plus a checksum, cut into 11-bit word indexes.

long: In a 12-word BIP39 phrase, the last word carries 7 entropy bits plus the 4 checksum bits. So only about 1 in 16 random 12-word combinations is valid; with 24 words the checksum is 8 bits, about 1 in 256. BIP39 lists the short checksum as a shortcoming: it misses 1 in 256 errors and can't correct them. Practical lesson: you can't invent a seed from words you like; let a trusted wallet's random generator create it.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #3: In a 12-word BIP39 phrase the last word holds 7 entropy bits + the 4 checksum bits, so only about 1 in 16 random 12-word combos is valid. With 24 words the checksum is 8 bits: about 1 in 256.

BIP39 itself lists the short checksum as a shortcoming: it misses 1 in 256 errors and can't correct them.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #3: You can't pick 12 random words as a seed: the last word partly works as a checksum, so only about 1 in 16 random 12-word combos is valid.

And even a valid one made of words you like isn't random enough. Let a trusted wallet's random generator create it, never your imagination.

card.title: Most random word lists are not valid seeds
card.sub: The last word holds a checksum, so you can't invent a seed from words you like.

long: The English BIP39 wordlist was designed so that the first four letters are enough to identify each word unambiguously, and similar words are avoided. Wallet input screens can autocomplete from 4 letters, and handwritten or engraved metal backups can store just 4-letter prefixes. That makes backups shorter and less error-prone, which matters because a backup you can't read back correctly is no backup.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #4: BIP39's English wordlist is built so the first four letters unambiguously identify each word, and similar-looking words are avoided.

Wallet input screens can autocomplete from 4 letters, and handwritten or engraved metal backups can store just 4-letter prefixes. Shorter backups, fewer reading errors.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #4: Handy detail for backups: in the English BIP39 list, the first 4 letters of each word are enough to identify it.

That makes a handwritten or engraved backup shorter and less error-prone. It matters: a backup you can't read back correctly is no backup at all.

card.title: Four letters are enough for each word
card.sub: Backups can store just 4-letter prefixes: shorter and less error-prone.

long: The 12 or 24 words are not the key itself. BIP39 turns the mnemonic (NFKD-normalized) into a seed with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512, salt = "mnemonic" + optional passphrase, 2048 iterations, giving 512 bits. That seed is the input to BIP32 master key generation, and every key and address is derived from it. This is why the exact words, and the passphrase if any, are what must be backed up.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #5: The 12 or 24 words are not the key itself. BIP39 seed = PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512(mnemonic in NFKD, salt = "mnemonic" + optional passphrase, 2048 iterations), giving 512 bits.

That seed feeds BIP32 master key generation, and every key and address is derived from it. So the exact words, and passphrase if any, are what you back up.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #5: Your 12 or 24 words are not your key directly. The wallet runs them through a hash function 2048 times to make a 512-bit seed.

Every key and address is derived from that seed. That's why the exact words, plus the passphrase if you use one, are what must be backed up.

card.title: The words are not the key itself
card.sub: PBKDF2 turns the phrase and optional passphrase into the seed behind every key.

long: The BIP39 passphrase ("25th word") is part of the PBKDF2 salt, so every passphrase produces a valid, different wallet. BIP39 calls this plausible deniability. The danger: there is no wrong passphrase error. A single typo opens another valid wallet that is simply empty. If the passphrase is lost or misremembered, the funds are unreachable, so it must be backed up as carefully as the words.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #6: The BIP39 passphrase ("25th word") is part of the PBKDF2 salt, so every passphrase yields a valid, different wallet. BIP39 calls this plausible deniability.

The danger: there's no wrong-passphrase error. A single typo opens another valid wallet that is simply empty. Lose the passphrase and the funds are unreachable.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #6: A BIP39 passphrase (the "25th word") creates a completely different wallet. There is no "wrong" passphrase: a typo just opens another valid, empty wallet.

If you lose or misremember it, the funds are out of reach for good. Back it up as carefully as the words themselves.
variant:
Crypto #Wallet Security #6: No such thing as a wrong passphrase: type one letter differently and your wallet opens fine, just empty. It's a different wallet.

Every passphrase leads to a valid wallet, so nothing warns you of the mistake. Back up the passphrase as carefully as the words, or the funds are gone.

card.title: The 25th word has no wrong answer
card.sub: A typo opens another valid, empty wallet. Back up the passphrase like the words.

long: BIP39 derives the seed from the mnemonic sentence itself, not from the raw entropy. Translating a phrase into another wordlist, for example English to Spanish, therefore gives a completely different seed. BIP39 lists this as a known shortcoming and strongly discourages non-English wordlists since most wallets support only English. Keep the phrase in the language and wordlist it was created with.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #7: BIP39 derives the seed from the mnemonic sentence itself, not from the raw entropy. Translating a phrase into another wordlist, e.g. English to Spanish, gives a completely different seed.

BIP39 lists this as a known shortcoming and strongly discourages non-English wordlists, since most wallets support only English.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #7: Same words, other language, different wallet. BIP39 hashes the words themselves, so a phrase "translated" into another wordlist gives a totally different seed.

Most wallets only support English anyway. Keep your phrase in the language and wordlist it was created with.

card.title: Translating your seed changes your wallet
card.sub: The seed comes from the sentence itself. Keep its original language and wordlist.

long: BIP32 hierarchical deterministic (HD) wallets: I = HMAC-SHA512(key = "Bitcoin seed", data = seed). The left 256 bits are the master private key, the right 256 bits the chain code. Child keys are derived by index, building a tree of keys from one root. Result: a single backup of the seed restores every address the wallet has used or will use.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #8: BIP32 HD wallets: I = HMAC-SHA512(key = "Bitcoin seed", data = seed). The left 256 bits are the master private key, the right 256 bits the chain code.

Child keys are derived by index, building a tree of keys from one root. A single backup of the seed restores every address the wallet has used or will use.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #8: One phrase, unlimited addresses. HD wallets grow a whole tree of keys from a single seed.

Each new address is a branch computed from that root, always the same way. So one backup restores every address you have used or will use, with no need to back up each new one.

card.title: One seed, a whole tree of keys
card.sub: BIP32 derives every key from one root, so a single backup restores every address.

long: Under BIP32, an extended public key (xpub) can derive all non-hardened child public keys. It cannot spend, since spending needs private keys, but it reveals every address in that account and its full balance and history. Sharing an xpub is a privacy decision: give it only to tools you trust, such as your own watch-only app.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #9: Under BIP32, an extended public key (xpub) can derive all non-hardened child public keys. It can't spend: spending needs private keys.

But it reveals every address in that account and its full balance and history. Sharing an xpub is a privacy decision: give it only to tools you trust, like your own watch-only app.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #9: Your "xpub" (extended public key) can't spend, but it reveals every address in that account and its whole history.

Anyone holding it can watch your balance and every payment in and out. Share it only with tools you trust, like your own watch-only app.

card.title: An xpub can't spend, but it sees everything
card.sub: It reveals every address, balance and history in the account. Share it carefully.

long: A lesser-known BIP32 property: a parent xpub plus any one non-hardened child private key is equivalent to the parent xprv. The child key is k_child = k_parent + IL, and IL can be computed from the xpub and chain code, so subtracting it gives the parent private key, and from it every key below. Treat xpubs as sensitive, especially if any child key could leak.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #10: A lesser-known BIP32 property: a parent xpub plus any one non-hardened child private key is equivalent to the parent xprv.

The child key is k_child = k_parent + IL, and IL is computable from the xpub and chain code, so subtracting it gives the parent private key, and every key below. Treat xpubs as sensitive.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #10: Surprising fact: someone with your xpub plus ONE leaked private key from a normal (non-hardened) child can compute the parent private key, and from it every key below.

The xpub isn't harmless on its own once any child key could leak. Treat it as sensitive data.

card.title: One leaked child key can expose the parent
card.sub: With the xpub and chain code, a non-hardened child key gives back the parent key.

long: BIP32 hardened children (index >= 2^31, written i' or iH) are derived from the parent private key rather than the public key, so they can't be computed from an xpub. That blocks the xpub + leaked child key attack at that level. This is why derivation paths like m/84'/0'/0' use hardened steps at the top: one leaked key can't climb back up the tree.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #11: BIP32 hardened children (index ≥ 2^31, written i' or iH) are derived from the parent private key, not the public key, so they can't be computed from an xpub.

That blocks the xpub + leaked child key attack at that level. It's why paths like m/84'/0'/0' use hardened steps at the top.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #11: That's why wallets use "hardened" steps (the ' in m/84'/0'/0') at the top of the path.

Those keys can't be computed from public data, only from the private key above them. So a leaked key can't climb back up past those hardened levels to the keys above.

card.title: Hardened paths stop keys climbing the tree
card.sub: Hardened children need the parent private key, so an xpub can't compute them.

long: BIP44 defines a standard path: m / purpose' / coin_type' / account' / change / address_index. coin_type comes from the SLIP-44 registry (Bitcoin 0, Ethereum 60). change is 0 for receiving addresses and 1 for change addresses. Wallets that follow it find the same keys from the same seed; the same seed on a different path gives different addresses.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #12: BIP44 defines a standard path: m / purpose' / coin_type' / account' / change / address_index. coin_type comes from the SLIP-44 registry (Bitcoin 0, Ethereum 60).

change is 0 for receiving addresses and 1 for change addresses. Wallets that follow it find the same keys from the same seed.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #12: Wallets agree on where your keys are with a path like m/44'/0'/0'/0/0: purpose, coin, account, receive or change, address number.

Two wallets that follow the same path find the same keys from the same seed. Same seed + different path = different addresses.

card.title: A standard map for every key in your seed
card.sub: Same seed, same path, same keys. A different path gives different addresses.

long: Bitcoin wallets use different purpose levels for different address types: 44' legacy, 49' nested SegWit, 84' native SegWit (bc1q), 86' Taproot (bc1p). Restoring a seed on the wrong path shows a zero balance even though the funds are safe. Fix: check the path or use an output descriptor. Never type the seed into a website that offers to recover it.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #13: Bitcoin wallets use different purpose levels per address type: 44' legacy, 49' nested SegWit, 84' native SegWit (bc1q), 86' Taproot (bc1p).

Restoring a seed on the wrong path shows a zero balance even though the funds are safe. Fix: check the path or use an output descriptor. Never type the seed into a "recovery" website.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #13: Restored your seed and see a zero balance? Don't panic: the wallet may be scanning another address type.

Each type, from old addresses to bc1q and bc1p, lives on its own path. Check which one you used. And never type your seed into a website that offers to "recover" it.

card.title: Zero balance after restore? Check the path
card.sub: Legacy, SegWit and Taproot use different purpose levels. Your funds are still safe.

long: BIP44 sets the address gap limit at 20: during recovery, a wallet stops scanning a chain after 20 consecutive unused addresses. Funds received past that gap still belong to the seed, but stay invisible after a restore until the wallet is told to scan further. Relevant if you generated many addresses without using them.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #14: BIP44 sets the address gap limit at 20: during recovery, a wallet stops scanning a chain after 20 consecutive unused addresses.

Funds received past that gap still belong to the seed, but stay invisible after a restore until the wallet is told to scan further. Relevant if you generated many unused addresses.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #14: Wallets stop looking after 20 unused addresses in a row, the BIP44 "gap limit".

If you created lots of addresses without using them, later funds may not appear after a restore. They're still yours: tell the wallet to scan further and they show up again.

card.title: Funds past the gap limit stay invisible
card.sub: Recovery stops after 20 unused addresses in a row. Tell the wallet to scan further.

long: Bitcoin spends whole UTXOs: when you pay part of a balance, the remainder goes to a change output. BIP44 keeps change addresses on a separate internal chain (change = 1). The seed covers them, but a tool that scans only the receiving chain (0) will miss those funds, and the balance will look wrong.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #15: Bitcoin spends whole UTXOs: when you pay part of a balance, the remainder goes to a change output. BIP44 keeps change addresses on a separate internal chain (change = 1).

The seed covers them, but a tool that scans only the receiving chain (0) will miss those funds, and the balance will look wrong.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #15: When you send part of a Bitcoin balance, the rest comes back to you at a new address of yours. That's "change".

Your seed covers it too, but those addresses live on their own branch. A tool that ignores change addresses can miss funds and show a wrong balance.

card.title: Change addresses hide part of your balance
card.sub: Change sits on a separate chain; a tool scanning only receiving addresses misses it.

long: Not every 12-word phrase is BIP39. Electrum 2.0+ seeds mark their type with a version prefix in a hash of the phrase instead of a BIP39 checksum, and derive the seed with the PBKDF2 salt "electrum" + passphrase. An Electrum phrase entered in a BIP39-only wallet gives a different, empty wallet. Write down which app created your seed.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #16: Not every 12-word phrase is BIP39. Electrum 2.0+ seeds mark their type with a version prefix in a hash of the phrase, not a BIP39 checksum, and derive the seed with the PBKDF2 salt "electrum" + passphrase.

An Electrum phrase entered in a BIP39-only wallet gives a different, empty wallet.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #16: Not every 12-word phrase is BIP39. Electrum uses its own seed format, so an Electrum phrase typed into a BIP39-only wallet gives a different, empty wallet.

The words look the same, but they're turned into a seed differently. Write down which app made your seed, next to the backup.

card.title: Not every 12-word phrase is BIP39
card.sub: An Electrum seed in a BIP39-only wallet opens an empty wallet. Note the app used.

long: BIP85 derives entropy from a BIP32 keychain at hardened paths under m/83696968' and turns it into new mnemonics or keys. One master seed can thus produce many independent child seeds (for a phone wallet, for example) with no new randomness to back up. A leaked child cannot reveal the parent, but the parent seed recreates every child, so the master backup is critical.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #17: BIP85 derives entropy from a BIP32 keychain at hardened paths under m/83696968' and turns it into new mnemonics or keys.

One master seed can produce many independent child seeds, e.g. for a phone wallet, with no new randomness to back up. A leaked child can't reveal the parent, but the parent recreates every child.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #17: One master backup can make many child seeds. BIP85 lets a wallet derive fresh, independent recovery phrases from your main seed, say for a phone wallet.

A leaked child phrase can't expose the main seed. But the main seed recreates all of them, so its backup is the one that really matters.

card.title: One master seed, many child seeds
card.sub: BIP85 needs no new backups, but the master recreates every child: guard it.

long: SLIP-39 standardizes Shamir's secret sharing for wallet backups: a master secret is split into N shares, any T of which reconstruct it, with up to 16 shares per group. Knowledge of fewer than T shares leaks no information about the secret. Example: 5 shares, any 3 restore. Lose 2 and you can still recover; a thief who finds 2 learns nothing. Shares should be kept in different places.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #18: SLIP-39 standardizes Shamir's secret sharing for wallet backups: a master secret is split into N shares, any T of which reconstruct it, up to 16 shares per group.

Fewer than T shares leak no information about the secret. Example: 5 shares, any 3 restore. Lose 2 and you still recover; a thief with 2 learns nothing.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #18: Shamir backup splits a wallet secret into shares, e.g. 5 shares where any 3 restore it. Lose 2, still fine. A thief who finds 2 learns nothing.

Below the threshold, the shares reveal nothing at all about the secret. Keep them in different places so one fire or one burglary can't take enough.

card.title: Shamir backups: any T of N shares restore
card.sub: Fewer shares than the threshold leak nothing, so a thief who finds 2 learns nothing.

long: SLIP-39 supports two levels: a group threshold over up to 16 groups, and a member threshold within each group (up to 16 shares). Example: 2 of 3 groups needed, one group being any 2 of 3 family members. Every share of one set starts with the same first words (random identifier and iteration exponent), so shares from different sets can't be mixed by mistake.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #19: SLIP-39 supports two levels: a group threshold over up to 16 groups, and a member threshold within each group (up to 16 shares). Example: 2 of 3 groups, one group being any 2 of 3 family members.

Every share of one set starts with the same first words, so shares from different sets can't be mixed by mistake.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #19: Shamir backups can be layered: for example you need 2 of 3 groups, and one group is "any 2 of 3 family members". SLIP-39 allows up to 16 groups.

All shares from one backup start with the same words, so you can't mix them up with shares from another backup by mistake.

card.title: Two levels of thresholds for family backups
card.sub: Groups and members each have a threshold, and shared first words keep sets apart.

long: SLIP-39 shares are not BIP39 phrases. They use a 1024-word list (10 bits per word), end with a 3-word RS1024 checksum, and are 20 words for a 128-bit secret or 33 words for 256 bits. The spec says it is for the most part not compatible with BIP39. Before relying on a Shamir backup, check that the wallet you would restore with supports SLIP-39.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #20: SLIP-39 shares are not BIP39 phrases. They use a 1024-word list (10 bits per word), end with a 3-word RS1024 checksum, and are 20 words for a 128-bit secret or 33 words for 256 bits.

The spec says it's for the most part not compatible with BIP39. Check your restore wallet supports SLIP-39.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #20: A Shamir share is not a BIP39 phrase: it uses its own 1024-word list and is 20 or 33 words long.

A BIP39-only wallet won't know what to do with it. Check that the wallet you'd restore with supports SLIP-39 before relying on it, not on the day you need it.

card.title: Shamir shares are not BIP39 phrases
card.sub: A 1024-word list and a checksum. Check your restore wallet supports SLIP-39.

long: Cutting a 24-word phrase into 3 piles of 8 is a bad backup. Anyone holding 2 piles faces at most 88 unknown bits instead of 256, and losing a single pile can block recovery. SLIP-39 shares below threshold reveal nothing about the secret, and multisig spreads keys properly. Use a proper scheme instead of splitting the words yourself.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #21: Naive splitting leaks entropy: cut 24 words into 3 piles of 8 and anyone holding 2 piles faces at most 88 unknown bits instead of 256, while losing one pile can block recovery.

SLIP-39 shares below threshold reveal nothing about the secret, and multisig spreads keys properly. Use a real scheme.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #21: Don't cut your 24 words into 3 piles of 8 yourself. Each pile hands a thief part of the secret, and losing one pile can lock you out.

With two piles, a thief faces about 88 unknown bits instead of 256: a needless weakening. Shamir backups or multisig do this job properly: below the threshold, nothing leaks.

card.title: Cutting your seed into piles is a bad backup
card.sub: Two piles leave few unknown bits, and losing one can block recovery.

long: Multisig requires several keys to sign, e.g. 2 of 3, so one stolen or lost key is not fatal. To restore an M-of-N Bitcoin multisig you need M seeds and the wallet's configuration: all N xpubs and the script type, usually stored as an output descriptor. Back up the descriptor with every key, and keep each key on a different device in a different place.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #22: Multisig requires several keys to sign, e.g. 2 of 3, so one stolen or lost key isn't fatal.

To restore an M-of-N Bitcoin multisig you need M seeds AND the wallet's setup: all N xpubs and the script type, usually stored as an output descriptor. Back up the descriptor with every key.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #22: Multisig means several keys must sign, e.g. 2 of 3. One stolen or lost key is not fatal.

Keep each key on a different device in a different place, or it's one key with extra steps. And back up the wallet's setup with every key: seeds alone aren't enough to restore it.

card.title: Restoring multisig takes more than seeds
card.sub: You also need every xpub and the script type. Back up the descriptor with each key.

long: MuSig2 (BIP327) aggregates n public keys into a single Schnorr public key. A Taproot output using that key looks the same on-chain as a single-signer output, so observers can't tell a group signed. Note MuSig2 is n-of-n: other thresholds need Taproot script paths or other schemes.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #23: MuSig2 (BIP327) aggregates n public keys into a single Schnorr public key.

A Taproot output using that key looks the same on-chain as a single-signer output, so observers can't tell a group signed. MuSig2 is n-of-n: other thresholds need Taproot script paths or other schemes.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #23: With Taproot and MuSig2, a group wallet can look exactly like a one-person wallet on the blockchain. Observers can't tell several people signed.

The catch: MuSig2 needs every member to sign. For "2 of 3" style rules, Taproot script paths or other schemes are needed.

card.title: A group signature that looks like one key
card.sub: MuSig2 makes n keys look like a single signer on-chain. It is n-of-n only.

long: Taproot (BIP341), activated in November 2021, makes outputs commit to a key plus a hidden tree of scripts. A key-path spend reveals no script at all; a script-path spend reveals only the branch used. Backup, recovery and inheritance conditions therefore stay private unless they are actually used.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #24: Taproot (BIP341), activated in November 2021, makes outputs commit to a key plus a hidden tree of scripts.

A key-path spend reveals no script at all; a script-path spend reveals only the branch used. Backup, recovery and inheritance conditions stay private unless they're actually used.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #24: Taproot, Bitcoin's November 2021 upgrade, keeps backup spending rules private.

An output can hide several conditions, like a recovery key or an inheritance plan. When you spend, only the condition you actually used is revealed, and the other branches stay hidden.

card.title: Recovery rules that stay private until used
card.sub: Taproot reveals no script on a key-path spend, and only the used branch otherwise.

long: A hardware signer keeps the private key on the device and only exports signatures. The host computer builds an unsigned transaction (in Bitcoin, a PSBT, BIP174) and the device checks and signs it. Malware on the computer can't simply copy the key. It can still try to get the user to approve a bad transaction, which is why the device screen matters.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #25: A hardware signer keeps the private key on the device and only exports signatures. The host builds an unsigned transaction (in Bitcoin, a PSBT, BIP174) and the device checks and signs it.

Malware on the computer can't simply copy the key. It can still try to get the user to approve a bad transaction.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #25: A hardware wallet keeps your keys on a small device that never hands them to your computer. The computer prepares the transaction, the device signs it.

Malware on the PC can't just copy the key. It can still try to trick you into approving a bad transaction, which is why the device screen matters.

card.title: The key stays on the device
card.sub: The computer builds the transaction; the hardware signer checks it and signs.

long: If the computer is compromised, the hardware wallet's display is the last honest view of the transaction. NCC Group's analysis of the Bybit hack notes that hardware wallets that clear-sign can expose malicious data even when the laptop is compromised. Rule: check the full address, amount and action on the device itself before confirming.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #26: If the computer is compromised, the hardware wallet's display is the last honest view of the transaction.

NCC Group's analysis of the Bybit hack notes that hardware wallets that clear-sign can expose malicious data even when the laptop is compromised. Check the full address, amount and action on the device itself.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #26: Golden rule: trust the hardware wallet's screen, not your computer's.

If your computer is infected, it can show you anything. The device screen is the last honest view. Check the full address, amount and action on the device itself before you confirm.

card.title: Trust the device screen, not the laptop
card.sub: Check the full address, amount and action on the hardware wallet before confirming.

long: Clipper malware watches the clipboard for crypto addresses and swaps in the attacker's. In February 2019 ESET reported the first clipper found on Google Play, posing as MetaMask and replacing copied BTC and ETH addresses. Defense: always compare the pasted address, ideally on a separate trusted screen such as a hardware wallet, before sending.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #27: Clipper malware watches the clipboard for crypto addresses and swaps in the attacker's.

In Feb 2019 ESET reported the first clipper found on Google Play, posing as MetaMask and replacing copied BTC and ETH addresses. Defense: always compare the pasted address, ideally on a separate trusted screen like a hardware wallet.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #27: Clipper malware watches your clipboard. You copy a crypto address, it pastes the attacker's instead.

In 2019 one was even found on Google Play, disguised as MetaMask. Always compare the pasted address before sending, ideally on a hardware wallet screen.

card.title: Malware that swaps the address you copied
card.sub: Clipper malware replaces copied addresses. Compare what you paste before sending.

long: PSBT (BIP174) packages everything an offline signer needs: inputs, UTXO data, derivation paths. long: January 2020: Kraken Security Labs showed it could extract encrypted seeds from Trezor One and Model T devices via voltage glitching, with under 15 minutes of physical access. Because the flaw is in the hardware, it can't be fixed by software. The recommended mitigation was a BIP39 passphrase. Lesson: physical access matters, and a strong passphrase still protects funds.

card.title: A hardware flaw no update can fix
card.sub: Voltage glitching extracted encrypted seeds; a strong BIP39 passphrase still protects.

long: Since every BIP39 passphrase opens a valid wallet, one phrase can host a decoy (no passphrase, small balance) and a hidden wallet behind a passphrase. BIP39 calls this plausible deniability. simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #30: A passphrase can act as a decoy: keep a small amount in the no-passphrase wallet and the rest behind the passphrase.

Both open from the same words. If someone forces you to open your wallet, there is a plausible one to show, and nothing proves another exists.

card.title: A decoy wallet for a forced unlock
card.sub: No passphrase opens a small balance; the real funds hide behind a passphrase.

card.sub: A phished account pushed malicious library code to many dApps. Read what you sign.

Users didn't do anything wrong: they just got the update. A browser extension shares your browser's risks, so keep long-term savings elsewhere.

card.sub: A bad extension version drained 2,596 wallets. Updates are a supply-chain path.

card.sub: Slope sent recovery phrases in plain text to a monitoring service.

long: A brainwallet derives the private key as SHA-256 of a passphrase the user thought up. At DEF CON 23 (2015), Ryan Castellucci showed with his brainflayer tool that attackers test huge lists of phrases at high speed and sweep any funded address. Human-chosen phrases are not random enough; never build a wallet from a sentence you made up.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #36: A brainwallet derives the private key as SHA-256 of a passphrase the user thought up.

At DEF CON 23 (2015), Ryan Castellucci showed with his brainflayer tool that attackers test huge lists of phrases at high speed and sweep any funded address. Human-chosen phrases aren't random enough.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #36: Never make a wallet from a phrase you thought up. "Brain wallets" built from memorable sentences get found and emptied by bots.

Attackers test huge lists of phrases at high speed, and sweep any address with funds. Humans are terrible random number generators.

card.title: Never build a wallet from a sentence
card.sub: Attackers test huge lists of human-chosen phrases and sweep any funded address.

long: Milk Sad (CVE-2023-39910): Libbitcoin Explorer 3.x's "bx seed" command used the Mersenne Twister PRNG seeded with only 32 bits, about 4.3 billion possibilities. Every wallet it ever generated can be enumerated by a computer. Thefts began on July 12, 2023. A seed is only as strong as the randomness behind it.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #37: Milk Sad (CVE-2023-39910): Libbitcoin Explorer 3.x's "bx seed" command used the Mersenne Twister PRNG seeded with only 32 bits, about 4.3 billion possibilities.

simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #37: "Milk Sad" (2023): a wallet command-line tool made seeds from only 32 bits of randomness, about 4.3 billion options. A computer can try them all.

And attackers did: funds were stolen starting July 2023. Your seed is only as strong as the randomness that created it.

card.title: A seed is only as strong as its randomness
card.sub: Milk Sad had about 4.3 billion possible seeds, and every one can be enumerated.

long: Profanity, a popular vanity address generator, had flawed key generation: 1inch showed its keys could be brute-forced. The warning was published on September 15, 2022. On September 20, Wintermute lost about $160M from a 0x0000000 vanity address that was likely made with Profanity. A nice-looking address is worthless if the key behind it is weak.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #38: Profanity, a popular vanity address generator, had flawed key generation: 1inch showed its keys could be brute-forced, in a warning published Sept 15, 2022.

simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #38: Vanity addresses (0x0000...) look cool, but keys made by the popular Profanity generator could be brute-forced.

In Sept 2022 researchers warned; five days later a firm using a vanity address lost about $160M. A pretty address is worthless if its key is weak.

card.title: A pretty address with a weak key
card.sub: Profanity's vanity keys could be brute-forced, and Wintermute lost funds days later.

long: Randstorm (Unciphered, November 2023): web wallets built with BitcoinJS-era code between 2011 and 2015 relied on browser randomness that could be weak, so some of their keys may be brute-forceable today. Anyone holding funds on a wallet created that way and in that period should consider moving them to a fresh seed.
tech:

simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #39: Old web wallet? 2023 research ("Randstorm") found that wallets made with BitcoinJS-based web apps between 2011 and 2015 may have weak randomness.

Some of those keys may be guessable today. If yours is that old, consider moving the funds to a fresh seed.

card.title: Old web wallets may have weak keys
card.sub: Randstorm: some keys from BitcoinJS-era web wallets may be brute-forceable today.

long: August 2013: Android's Java SecureRandom could produce repeated values, so some Bitcoin apps reused the ECDSA nonce k. Two signatures with the same k reveal the private key, and attackers stole funds. Wallet apps shipped fixes and moved users to new keys. A flaw in the system random generator broke wallets that were otherwise correct.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #40: Aug 2013: Android's Java SecureRandom could produce repeated values, so some Bitcoin apps reused the ECDSA nonce k. Two signatures with the same k reveal the private key, and attackers stole funds.

Wallet apps shipped fixes and moved users to new keys. A flaw in the system RNG broke wallets that were otherwise correct.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #40: Aug 2013: a flaw in Android's random number generator let attackers steal from Bitcoin wallet apps.

Repeated randomness in signatures leaked private keys, and apps had to move users to new keys. The wallets' own code was fine; the phone's randomness wasn't.

card.title: When the phone's random generator failed
card.sub: Repeated ECDSA nonces revealed private keys, and attackers stole funds from apps.

long: ECDSA signing computes s = k^-1(z + r*d) with a one-time secret nonce k. If two signatures share k, anyone can compute k = (z1 - z2)/(s1 - s2) and then the private key d. fail0verflow used this in 2010 to recover Sony's PS3 signing key, since Sony used a static k. RFC 6979 avoids the problem by deriving k deterministically from the key and the message.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #41: ECDSA signing computes s = k^-1(z + r*d) with a one-time secret nonce k. If two signatures share k, anyone can compute k = (z1 - z2)/(s1 - s2), then the private key d.

fail0verflow used this in 2010 to recover Sony's PS3 signing key: Sony used a static k. RFC 6979 avoids it by deriving k from the key and message.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #41: Every ECDSA signature uses a one-time secret number. Reuse it once and anyone can compute the private key from the two signatures.

That's how Sony's PS3 signing key was recovered in 2010. The RFC 6979 fix: derive that number from the key and the message, so it can't repeat by accident.

card.title: Reuse a nonce once and the key is gone
card.sub: Two signatures with the same k give away the private key. RFC 6979 prevents it.

source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6979 (k déterministe, HMAC_DRBG) + https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_Curve_Digital_Signature_Algorithm (fail0verflow, déc. 2010, k statique chez Sony) + https://www.exophase.com/20540/hackers-describe-ps3-security-as-epic-fail-gain-unrestricted-access/ (27C3, 29/12/2010)

long: secp256k1 has a group order n of about 1.16 x 10^77, so a properly random 256-bit private key can't be brute-forced. Keys cracked in practice came from weak entropy (brainwallets, Milk Sad, Profanity) or nonce reuse, not from breaking the math. Real attacks target people, random generators and signatures.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #42: secp256k1 has a group order n of about 1.16 x 10^77, so a properly random 256-bit private key can't be brute-forced.

Keys cracked in practice came from weak entropy (brainwallets, Milk Sad, Profanity) or nonce reuse, not from breaking the math. Real attacks target people, random generators and signatures.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #42: Guessing someone's key is hopeless: there are about 10^77 possible private keys.

The keys cracked in practice came from shortcuts: a human-chosen phrase, a weak random generator, or a reused signature number. Real thefts target people and bad tools, not the math.

card.title: Nobody breaks the math, they break people
card.sub: Cracked keys came from weak entropy or nonce reuse, not from brute force.

long: EIP-55 (2016) adds a checksum to Ethereum addresses through letter case, based on the Keccak-256 hash of the lowercase address. That gives about 15 check bits on average; a mistyped address passes by accident only about 0.0247% of the time. It catches typos, but not a scammer's address that is itself valid, such as one pasted from a poisoned history.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #43: EIP-55 (2016) adds a checksum to Ethereum addresses through letter case, based on the Keccak-256 hash of the lowercase address: about 15 check bits on average.

A mistyped address passes by accident only about 0.0247% of the time. It catches typos, but not a valid scammer's address, like one pasted from a poisoned history.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #43: Ever noticed Ethereum addresses mix upper and lower case? That's a checksum (EIP-55). Most typos get flagged by your wallet.

But it can't help if you paste a scammer's address that is itself valid, for example one copied from a poisoned transaction history.

card.title: Capital letters that catch typos
card.sub: EIP-55 catches mistyped addresses, not a valid scam address pasted from your history.

long: Bech32 (BIP173), used by bc1 Bitcoin addresses, guarantees detection of any error affecting at most 4 characters, and has very low odds of missing larger errors. Taproot addresses (bc1p) use the updated Bech32m (BIP350). Typos are handled; lookalike scam addresses are a different problem the checksum can't solve.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #44: Bech32 (BIP173), used by bc1 Bitcoin addresses, guarantees detection of any error affecting at most 4 characters, with very low odds of missing larger errors.

Taproot addresses (bc1p) use the updated Bech32m (BIP350). Typos are handled; lookalike scam addresses are a problem the checksum can't solve.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #44: Bitcoin bc1 addresses have a strong checksum: any mistake in up to 4 characters is guaranteed to be caught. Typos are handled.

Lookalike scam addresses are a different problem: they're valid addresses, just not yours. No checksum can tell you that you copied the wrong one.

card.title: Bech32 catches typos, not lookalikes
card.sub: Any error in up to 4 characters is detected. Scam addresses are another problem.

long: Address poisoning: attackers generate an address matching the first and last characters of one you often pay, then plant a lookalike transfer in your history. If you later copy the address from your history, you copy theirs. In May 2024 one victim lost about $68M this way. Defense: use a saved address book and check every character.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #45: Address poisoning: attackers generate an address matching the first and last characters of one you often pay, then plant a lookalike transfer in your history.

If you later copy the address from your history, you copy theirs. In May 2024 one victim lost about $68M this way. Defense: a saved address book and checking every character.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #45: Address poisoning: a scammer plants a lookalike transfer in your history, from an address that starts and ends like one you use.

Next time you copy from your history, you copy theirs. Use a saved address book instead of your history, and check every character, not just the start and end.

card.title: Poisoned history, copied scam address
card.sub: Lookalike transfers plant a fake address. Use an address book, check every character.

card.title: Checking start and end is not enough
card.sub: The scam address matched the first and last six characters. Nearly all was returned.

long: ERC-20 approve(spender, amount) sets an allowance that the spender can use through transferFrom at any time. Many apps request unlimited approvals (2^256 - 1), which stay active until revoked, even years later. If the approved contract is malicious or gets exploited, the approved balance is exposed. Review and revoke old approvals.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #47: ERC-20 approve(spender, amount) sets an allowance the spender can use through transferFrom at any time. Many apps request unlimited approvals (2^256 - 1), which stay active until revoked, even years later.

If the approved contract is malicious or gets exploited, the approved balance is exposed. Review and revoke old approvals.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #47: When you use a DEX, you "approve" it to spend your tokens. Many apps ask for unlimited approval, and it stays active until you revoke it, even years later.

If that app is ever hacked, your approved tokens can be taken without a new signature from you. Review and revoke old approvals.

card.title: Unlimited approvals stay active for years
card.sub: If the approved contract is malicious or exploited, the balance is exposed. Revoke.

long: ERC-721 setApprovalForAll(operator, true) authorizes an operator to transfer all of the owner's NFTs in that contract, now and later, until revoked. One signature covers the whole collection. A fake mint site asking for it is a classic drainer sign.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #48: ERC-721 setApprovalForAll(operator, true) authorizes an operator to transfer all of the owner's NFTs in that contract, now and later, until revoked.

One signature covers the whole collection, including NFTs you get later. A fake mint site asking for it is a classic drainer sign.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #48: NFT version: "setApprovalForAll" lets an operator move every NFT you own in that collection, now and later, until you revoke it.

One signature is enough to empty the whole collection. A fake mint site asking for it is a classic drainer sign: refuse.

card.title: One signature for your whole NFT collection
card.sub: setApprovalForAll lets an operator move every NFT in it. Fake mint sites ask for it.

long: EIP-2612 permit(owner, spender, value, deadline, v, r, s) sets a token allowance from an off-chain EIP-712 signature that anyone can submit on-chain. Signing costs no gas and shows nothing on-chain, which makes it feel harmless. Drainers ask for a permit, then call permit and transferFrom themselves. Free to sign does not mean safe to sign.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #49: EIP-2612 permit(owner, spender, value, deadline, v, r, s) sets a token allowance from an off-chain EIP-712 signature that anyone can submit on-chain.

Signing costs no gas and shows nothing on-chain, so it feels harmless. Drainers ask for a permit, then call permit and transferFrom themselves.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #49: A "permit" is a signature, not a transaction: no gas, nothing on-chain when you sign. But it can let someone spend your tokens.

Drainers collect the signature, then submit it themselves and take the tokens. Free to sign does not mean safe to sign.

card.title: Free to sign does not mean safe to sign
card.sub: A gasless permit signature lets drainers set an allowance and take your tokens.

long: Wallet drainers are phishing kits: a fake site or airdrop gets a wallet to connect, then requests the most valuable approval or permit it can. ScamSniffer's 2024 report (January 2025) counted about $494M stolen by wallet drainers that year, from about 332,000 addresses. A site pushing you to sign quickly is a warning sign.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #50: Wallet drainers are phishing kits: a fake site or airdrop gets a wallet to connect, then requests the most valuable approval or permit it can.

ScamSniffer's 2024 report (Jan 2025) counted about $494M stolen by wallet drainers that year, from about 332,000 addresses. A site pushing you to sign quickly is a warning sign.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #50: Wallet drainers are phishing kits: a fake site, a fake airdrop, a signature request.

ScamSniffer counted about $494M stolen this way in 2024, from about 332,000 addresses. The kit asks for the most valuable approval it can get. If a site pushes you to sign fast, close it.

card.title: Phishing kits built to empty wallets
card.sub: Drainers took funds from about 332,000 addresses in 2024. Rushed signing is a red flag.

long: EIP-191 personal_sign hashes "\x19Ethereum Signed Message:\n" + length + message before signing. RLP-encoded transactions never start with 0x19, so a signed text message can't be valid as a transaction. Signing a raw hash has no such guard, which is why raw hash signing requests are dangerous.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #51: EIP-191 personal_sign hashes "\x19Ethereum Signed Message:\n" + length + message before signing.

RLP-encoded transactions never start with 0x19, so a signed text message can't be valid as a transaction. Signing a raw hash has no such guard, which is why raw hash signing requests are dangerous.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #51: Why can't a "sign this message" request secretly be a transaction? Wallets add a fixed prefix ("Ethereum Signed Message") before signing text.

A transaction can never start that way, so the signature can't be reused as one. Requests to sign a raw hash skip that guard: treat them as dangerous.

card.title: Signed messages can't pass as transactions
card.sub: A prefix keeps text signatures safe. Raw hash signing requests have no such guard.

long: EIP-712 typed data: the wallet signs "\x19\x01" + domainSeparator + hashStruct(message). The domain (name, version, chainId, verifyingContract) binds the signature to one app and chain so it can't be replayed elsewhere. Wallets can show the fields (token, spender, amount, deadline) in readable form. Read them: the spender is who gets access.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #52: EIP-712 typed data: the wallet signs "\x19\x01" + domainSeparator + hashStruct(message).

The domain (name, version, chainId, verifyingContract) binds the signature to one app and chain so it can't be replayed elsewhere. Wallets can show the fields (token, spender, amount, deadline) in readable form.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #52: EIP-712 lets wallets show what you sign as readable fields (token, spender, amount, deadline) instead of a random-looking hash.

The signature is also tied to one app and one chain. Read those fields: "spender" is who gets access to your tokens.

card.title: Read the spender before you sign typed data
card.sub: The domain binds the signature to one app and chain. The spender gets the access.

long: Blind signing: when a hardware wallet can't parse calldata (or nested calls), it shows only a hash or raw hex, and the user approves without knowing what it does. NCC Group's Bybit analysis says blind signing is highly likely to occur. Prefer clear signing and decode calldata independently before approving.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #53: Blind signing: when a hardware wallet can't parse calldata (or nested calls), it shows only a hash or raw hex, and the user approves without knowing what it does.

NCC Group's Bybit analysis says blind signing is highly likely to occur. Prefer clear signing and decode calldata independently before approving.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #53: Blind signing: your hardware wallet shows a hash or raw data it can't decode, and you approve anyway.

It's like signing a contract in a language you can't read. Prefer wallets and apps that show the transaction in clear, and check it with another tool before approving.

card.title: Approving a transaction you can't read
card.sub: Blind signing shows only a hash or hex. Prefer clear signing and decode calldata.

Signers saw the original transaction; their devices showed raw data. The FBI attributed the theft to North Korea.

simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #56: Smart accounts: since 2023 (ERC-4337) an Ethereum wallet can be a smart contract with its own rules: spending limits, several keys, recovery.

Your actions go through a separate queue and a shared contract that runs them. No change to Ethereum itself was needed.

card.title: Wallets that run their own rules
card.sub: ERC-4337 lets a smart contract wallet set spending limits, several keys and recovery.

long: Social recovery wallets, described by Vitalik Buterin in January 2021: one signing key for daily use, plus 3 or more guardians, a majority of whom can replace that key if it is lost. Guardians don't sign payments, but a colluding majority could take over, so they should be people or devices unlikely to collude.

simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #57: Social recovery: with a smart account, trusted guardians (friends, family, your other devices) can together replace a lost signing key.

They can't spend your funds day to day. But a majority of them could take over, so choose guardians who won't collude.

card.title: Guardians who can replace a lost key
card.sub: A majority of guardians can restore access. Pick people unlikely to collude.

long: EIP-7702, live since the Pectra upgrade (May 7, 2025), adds transaction type 0x04 with an authorization list. Each authorization signs [chain_id, address, nonce] and writes a delegation indicator 0xef0100 + address to the account, whose calls then run that code. A normal account gains smart-wallet features while keeping its address.

simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #58: Since the Pectra upgrade (May 7, 2025), a normal Ethereum account can point to smart-contract code and gain smart-wallet features while keeping its address.

You sign an authorization naming the code, and from then on your account runs it. Same address, new abilities.

card.title: Smart-wallet features, same old address
card.sub: EIP-7702 lets a normal account delegate its calls to code while keeping its address.

long: EIP-7702 risk: delegated code has unrestricted access to the account. The spec says apps must not ask users to sign authorizations and that there is no safe way to provide this interface; wallets must audit delegate code. An authorization with chain_id 0 is valid on every chain. One signed authorization can hand full control of the account to an attacker.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #59: EIP-7702 risk: delegated code has unrestricted access to the account. The spec says apps must not ask users to sign authorizations: "there is no safe way to provide this interface".

Wallets must audit delegate code. An authorization with chain_id 0 is valid on every chain. One signature can hand over the account.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #59: The flip side of EIP-7702: one signed authorization can give an attacker's contract full control of your account.

The standard itself says websites should never ask for one. And if it's made for "any chain", it works on all of them at once. If a site asks you to sign one, refuse.

card.title: One authorization can hand over the account
card.sub: Delegated code has unrestricted access. Apps must not ask users to sign these.

long: EIP-7702 delegations are reversible with the account key: a new authorization overwrites the previous delegation, and delegating to the zero address clears the account's code, making it a plain account again. Delegations apply to one chain unless chain_id is 0.
tech:
Crypto #Wallet Security #60: EIP-7702 delegations are reversible with the account key: a new authorization overwrites the previous delegation.

Delegating to the zero address clears the account's code, making it a plain account again. Delegations apply to one chain unless chain_id is 0.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #60: Delegated your account with EIP-7702 and regret it? You can replace or remove the delegation by signing a new authorization with your key.

Pointing it to the zero address clears the code and makes it a plain account again. It only works if your key is still yours.

card.title: Delegations can be undone with the key
card.sub: A new authorization overwrites the old one; the zero address clears the code.

long: Soon after Pectra, Wintermute reported that the majority of EIP-7702 delegations pointed to copy-pasted sweeper contracts it tracks on a Dune dashboard as "CrimeEnjoyor". Attackers install them on accounts whose keys already leaked, so any funds sent there go straight to the attacker. Once a key has leaked, the address is burned.

simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #61: After Pectra, attackers used EIP-7702 on accounts whose keys had already leaked, installing "sweeper" code that sends their funds straight to the attacker.

Wintermute named this contract CrimeEnjoyor. Lesson: once a key has leaked, don't reuse the address. Move to a new one.

card.title: Once a key leaks, the address is burned
card.sub: Sweeper contracts send any funds arriving at leaked accounts straight to attackers.

Creditor repayments began in July 2024, a decade later. Coins left with a custodian depend on that custodian's security: not your keys, not your coins.

long: Cold storage means spending without the private keys ever being online (Bitcoin Wiki). Hot wallets, such as phone apps and browser extensions, keep keys on networked devices exposed to malware. Like a pocket and a safe: keep online only what you need soon, and keep savings offline.

Hot wallets, such as phone apps and browser extensions, keep keys on networked devices exposed to malware. Like a pocket and a safe: keep online only what you need soon, and keep savings offline.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #63: Hot wallet = keys on an internet-connected device, handy for daily spending. Cold storage = keys kept offline, never touching the internet.

Think pocket and safe: small amounts hot, savings cold. Malware can reach a phone or a browser, not a key that never goes online.

card.title: A pocket and a safe for your coins
card.sub: Keep online only what you need soon. Keep savings in cold storage, offline.

long: Section 10 of the Bitcoin whitepaper: "a new key pair should be used for each transaction to keep them from being linked to a common owner." HD wallets (BIP32) make this automatic by deriving a fresh address for each payment. Address reuse is a privacy leak, not a convenience.
tech:

HD wallets (BIP32) make this automatic by deriving a fresh address for each payment. Address reuse is a privacy leak, not a convenience.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #64: Using a fresh address for each payment isn't paranoia, it's in the Bitcoin whitepaper: a new key pair for each transaction keeps payments from being linked to one owner.

HD wallets do this for you, with a new address each time. Reusing one address lets anyone link your payments together.

card.title: A new address for every payment
card.sub: Address reuse links your payments. HD wallets derive a fresh address each time.

long: Dusting: someone sends tiny amounts to many addresses, hoping the owner later spends the dust together with other coins. Under the common-input-ownership heuristic (whitepaper section 10, multi-input transactions), that ties the addresses to one owner. Coin control lets you freeze unexpected dust as do-not-spend.

simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #65: Dust attack: someone sends tiny amounts to many addresses, hoping you later spend them together with your other coins.

Spending coins together suggests they belong to the same owner, which can link your addresses. Use your wallet's coin control to freeze unexpected dust.

card.title: Tiny deposits meant to unmask you
card.sub: Spending dust with other coins ties addresses together. Freeze it with coin control.

long: Bitcoin timelocks allow inheritance without handing over keys. OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY (BIP65, absolute) and OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY (BIP112, relative) let a script add a recovery key, for example an heir's, usable only after a set time. With Taproot that path stays hidden unless it is used.

That key is usable only after a set time. With Taproot, that path stays hidden unless it's used.
simple:
Crypto #Wallet Security #66: Inheritance without handing over your keys: Bitcoin timelocks can add a backup spending path that only opens after a set date, for example for an heir's key.

Until then, only you can spend. With Taproot, that backup path stays invisible on the blockchain unless it's actually used.

card.title: Inheritance without handing over keys
card.sub: Timelocks add an heir's recovery key usable only after a set time, hidden by Taproot.

long: Series recap: a wallet guards keys, not coins. Topics covered: BIP39/BIP32 seeds and passphrases, hardened paths, Shamir and multisig backups, weak-randomness failures, address poisoning, approvals and permits, blind signing, ERC-4337 and EIP-7702.
